title: Rabea Hinsching
text:
I am a PhD candidate in Economics at the University of East Anglia. My research is in applied microeconomics, with a focus on development, natural resources, and political economy. I am particularly interested in how firms, governments, and local institutions shape development outcomes, and how these processes affect communities.

My job market paper examines the developmental impact of mining companies’ social investments in South Africa’s Gauteng Province. You can find the latest draft here.
As part of my research, I collected data on mining companies’ social investments from corporate reports using a GPT-based algorithm. The code for the project is available on my GitHub. I am currently developing this dataset into a publicly accessible project tracker. An early version is available on this website under “CSI Tracker”.

March 2024 – present
I have teaching experience at both undergraduate and postgraduate level, including teaching Applied Methods for Impact Evaluation (PG) and Economics and Statistics for Economists (UG), as well as contributing to assessment and marking for Environmental Economics (UG) and Behavioural Finance (UG).




September 2023 – May 2026
The Brilliant Club is a university-access charity that works with schools and PhD researchers to provide young people with university-style learning and support their progression to higher education. I delivered both pre-designed and independently developed courses through teaching placements at local secondary schools.
My course, “What’s the Business of the Business?”, introduced students to questions around how businesses operate, the role of firms in society, and the economic and social consequences of business decisions.

title: Rabea Hinsching
text:
Current Papers

The Limits of Firm-Led Development: Evidence from South African Mining Communities
Draft  Type: Work in Progress (Job Market Paper/Thesis Chapter)
Abstract: Firm-led development initiatives have become more prominent in recent years, yet evidence of their effectiveness remains limited. This paper evaluates the impact of mining companies’ local economic development programmes (LEDs), which aim to increase incomes and reduce poverty in host communities by promoting alternative livelihood strategies and entrepreneurship. I compile a novel LED project database and combine it with seven waves of geo-coded household data from South Africa’s Gauteng Province. Using an event-study framework, I compare outcomes in LED-receiving areas before and after project implementation. The results show persistent improvements in food security and an increased likelihood of receiving an income. However, effects on entrepreneurship are short-lived, while employment and income remain unchanged. The results are largely driven by alternative livelihood programmes, which promote income diversification. The results suggest that LEDs can reduce markers of absolute deprivation, yet fall short of delivering fundamental change.


Corporate Social Investment, Political Participation, and Trust in Local Government
Draft available upon request  Type: Work in Progress (Thesis Chapter)  Abstract: Through Corporate Social Investment (CSI), companies seek to contribute to the development of their operating areas, taking over responsibilities usually held by local governments. This paper investigates whether CSI affects citizens’ government perception and political participation at the local level. I focus on mining-related CSI in South Africa’s Gauteng Province and combine information on CSI projects with household survey and electoral data. Using an event study design, I estimate the effects of CSI on political participation, as well as trust in and satisfaction with local government. The results suggest that CSI projects increase community-level political participation, measured by attendance of community meetings, but have no meaningful impact on government trust or satisfaction. CSI-receiving areas show higher participation in subsequent municipal and ward elections, suggesting spillovers to electoral participation. Together, these findings suggest that CSI can mobilise citizens to participate more actively in local politics without weakening trust in government institutions. 


Can Large-Scale Mining Promote Public Good Provision? Evidence from South Africa’s Mining Reform
Draft available upon request  Type: Work in Progress (Thesis Chapter)  Abstract: This paper examines whether mining can strengthen local service delivery when companies are required to invest in local public goods. I use South Africa as a case study, where post-apartheid reforms introduced such requirements alongside a fundamental overhaul of local governance and service delivery, providing a useful setting for examining their effects. Using census data from 2001 to 2022, I compare access to basic services across mining and non-mining municipalities, focusing on gold and platinum-group metal (PGM) mining and four services: electricity, water, sanitation, and refuse removal. I instrument for mining presence using municipalities’ overlap with exogenously determined mineral deposits and control for baseline levels of service provision. I find that PGM mining is associated with significantly higher access to basic services, while the evidence is weaker for gold mining. These effects are not explained by increases in municipal revenues or improvements in institutional quality. Instead, the results point to a more direct role for mining companies in expanding local service infrastructure, suggesting that corporate investment can help fill gaps in municipal service provision.

title: Rabea Hinsching
text:
This tracker started as part of my PhD research, where I collected data on corporate social investment (CSI) projects by mining companies. I thought it could be useful beyond my own work to show where and when these investments took place.
The tracker covers Gauteng Province and records projects between 2009 and 2024. Beyond its usefulness for research, it may also be of interest to mining-affected communities, mining companies, and policymakers.
It can help identify project overlaps between different mining companies, spot which areas are currently or historically underserved, and highlight which project types dominate or are lacking. It can also be used to assess how well investments align with municipalities’ integrated development plans and to track which projects were delayed or abandoned.
The tracker is still in beta while I finalise the dataset and ensure everything is properly referenced. Right now it covers Gauteng Province, but I plan to expand to the North West and Free State Province, and perhaps other countries in the future.
Find the current version of the tracker here
